narrative:
The model estimated a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means it judged failure more likely than success, though it also implies a 40% chance of passing, so this is a risk estimate rather than a certainty. Because admission was tied to that estimate, your application was rejected.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. The second strongest was your first-year standing: you were in the second decile versus an accepted average near the sixth, which also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential factor and, in this case, worked in your favor by pushing toward passing, even though at 2.50 it was still below the accepted average of 3.23. Your LSAT score of 31 was also below the accepted average of 37.18, though it was not among the top three drivers. Gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing, consider retaking the LSAT, and seek advising on a stronger reapplication. You can also ask for human review of the decision.
